### Chapter 16: Signals and Return Forecasts {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: sol-16-setup
#| include: false
source("R/_common.R")
library(tidypm)
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return
Re <- R - rf
N  <- ncol(Re); dates <- zoo::index(R)

# The chapter's signals, rebuilt so that this fragment runs on its own. The
# curve block is built for every region here, because exercise 1 needs it.
P   <- cumprod(1 + R)
mom <- xts::lag.xts(P, 1) / xts::lag.xts(P, 12) - 1
cv  <- sim_curve_weekly |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = series, values_from = value) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)
i_last  <- findInterval(dates, cv$date)
stopifnot(all(cv$date[i_last] <= dates), all(dates - cv$date[i_last] < 8))  # weeks are 6 to 8 days apart
regions <- c("CH", "EU", "JP", "UK", "US")
term_m  <- -as.matrix(cv[i_last, paste0(regions, "_Slope")])
ig_m    <- 100 * as.matrix(cv[i_last, paste0(regions, "_IG_Spread")])
colnames(term_m) <- paste0("term_", regions); colnames(ig_m) <- paste0("ig_", regions)
curve_all <- xts::xts(cbind(term_m, ig_m), order.by = dates)
turb <- uncertaintymeasures::OSturbulence(R, rolling = TRUE, roll.obs = 60)$turb
colnames(turb) <- "turb"
common_lag <- xts::lag.xts(merge(curve_all, turb), 1)
mom_lag    <- xts::lag.xts(mom, 1)

region_of <- function(s) { r <- sub("_.*", "", s); if (r == "GLOBAL") "US" else r }
pairs_of <- function(s, local = FALSE) {
  r <- if (local) region_of(s) else "US"
  data.frame(date = dates, y = as.numeric(Re[, s]), mom = as.numeric(mom_lag[, s]),
             term = as.numeric(common_lag[, paste0("term_", r)]),
             ig   = as.numeric(common_lag[, paste0("ig_", r)]),
             turb = as.numeric(common_lag[, "turb"]))
}

sig4 <- c("mom", "term", "ig", "turb")
burn <- 120L; oos <- seq.int(burn + 1L, nrow(Re))
nw_t <- function(m, j = 2L) {
  nw <- sandwich::NeweyWest(m, lag = 6, prewhite = FALSE)
  unname(stats::coef(m)[j] / sqrt(nw[j, j]))
}
ols_fc <- function(d, v, m) {
  tr <- which(!is.na(d[[v]]) & seq_len(nrow(d)) < m)
  b  <- stats::lm.fit(cbind(1, d[[v]][tr]), d$y[tr])$coefficients
  unname(b[1] + b[2] * d[[v]][m])
}
r2_os <- function(y, f, f0) 1 - sum((y - f)^2) / sum((y - f0)^2)
cw_t  <- function(y, f, f0) nw_t(stats::lm(I((y - f0)^2 - (y - f)^2 + (f0 - f)^2) ~ 1), 1L)

forecasts_of <- function(local = FALSE) {
  lapply(colnames(Re), function(s) {
    d <- pairs_of(s, local)
    out <- data.frame(date = dates[oos], series = s, y = d$y[oos],
                      mean = vapply(oos, function(m) mean(d$y[seq_len(m - 1L)]), numeric(1)))
    for (v in sig4) out[[v]] <- vapply(oos, function(m) ols_fc(d, v, m), numeric(1))
    out
  }) |> dplyr::bind_rows()
}
fc <- forecasts_of()
oos_of <- function(fc, model) {
  fc |>
    dplyr::group_by(series) |>
    dplyr::summarise(r2os = r2_os(y, .data[[model]], mean),
                     cw   = cw_t(y, .data[[model]], mean), .groups = "drop")
}

# The tilt and its accounting, as in the chapter, with kappa exposed.
vol60 <- zoo::rollapply(Re, 60, stats::sd, align = "right", fill = NA)
band  <- 0.5 / N
kappa0 <- band / (0.5 / sqrt(12))
w_policy <- setNames(rep(1 / N, N), colnames(Re))
tilt_weights <- function(fc, model, kappa = kappa0) {
  F  <- fc |> dplyr::select(date, series, f = dplyr::all_of(model)) |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = series, values_from = f)
  Fm <- as.matrix(F[, colnames(Re)])
  W  <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(Fm)), function(i) {
    s  <- Fm[i, ] / as.numeric(vol60[oos[i] - 1L, ]); s <- s - mean(s)
    tl <- pmin(pmax(kappa * s, -band), band)
    w  <- pmax(w_policy + tl - mean(tl), 0); w / sum(w)
  }, numeric(N)))
  dimnames(W) <- list(as.character(dates[oos]), colnames(Re)); W
}
cost_rate <- pm_costs_default()[sub(".*_", "", colnames(Re))]
names(cost_rate) <- colnames(Re)
run_path <- function(W) {
  Rm <- zoo::coredata(R)[oos, colnames(Re), drop = FALSE]
  r  <- rowSums(W * Rm)
  drifted <- W * (1 + Rm) / (1 + r)
  trade   <- abs(W[-1, , drop = FALSE] - drifted[-nrow(W), , drop = FALSE])
  tibble::tibble(gross = r, turnover = c(rowSums(trade) / 2, 0),
                 cost = c(as.numeric(trade %*% cost_rate), 0)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(net = gross - cost)
}
gamma <- 5
ce_of <- function(e) 12 * mean(e) - gamma / 2 * 12 * stats::var(e)
W_policy  <- matrix(1 / N, length(oos), N, dimnames = list(as.character(dates[oos]), colnames(Re)))
ce_policy <- ce_of(run_path(W_policy)$net - rf[oos])
```

#### Exercise 1

Each non-US series gets the term spread of its own region; the US series and
the commodity keep the US curve, so their rows cannot change.

```{r}
#| label: sol-16-ex1
fc_local <- forecasts_of(local = TRUE)
ex1 <- dplyr::inner_join(oos_of(fc, "term")       |> dplyr::select(series, us = r2os),
                         oos_of(fc_local, "term") |> dplyr::select(series, local = r2os),
                         by = "series") |>
  dplyr::mutate(difference = local - us) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(difference))
stopifnot(sum(ex1$difference < 0) > sum(ex1$difference > 0))   # the US curve wins more often
ex1 |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(-series, ~ sprintf("%+.2f%%", 100 * .x)))
c(local_better = sum(ex1$difference > 0), unchanged = sum(ex1$difference == 0),
  us_better = sum(ex1$difference < 0))
```

The local curve is the better forecaster on `r sum(ex1$difference > 0)` of
the `r sum(ex1$difference != 0)` series whose signal changed, and the US curve
on `r sum(ex1$difference < 0)`. The largest gain is `r ex1$series[1]`, whose
$R^2_{\text{OS}}$ moves from `r sprintf("%+.2f%%", 100 * ex1$us[1])` to
`r sprintf("%+.2f%%", 100 * ex1$local[1])`; the largest loss is
`r ex1$series[nrow(ex1)]`. A local bond was simulated from its local curve,
so the local slope is closer to the state that generated it, and it still
loses on most series. What @eq-16-r2os rewards is not closeness to the
mechanism but a slope that stays stable across the expanding window, and on
this sample the shared US spread has that property more often than the local
one. The economically obvious signal is not automatically the statistically
better one.

#### Exercise 2

The restriction replaces a negative forecast of an equity premium by zero, on
the argument that a risk premium cannot be negative.

```{r}
#| label: sol-16-ex2
eq  <- grep("_equity$", colnames(Re), value = TRUE)
ex2 <- fc |>
  dplyr::filter(series %in% eq) |>
  dplyr::mutate(term_ct = pmax(term, 0)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(series) |>
  dplyr::summarise(r2os = r2_os(y, term, mean), r2os_ct = r2_os(y, term_ct, mean),
                   cw = cw_t(y, term, mean), cw_ct = cw_t(y, term_ct, mean),
                   share_truncated = mean(term < 0), .groups = "drop")
# The full-sample slope of the term spread on each equity series, for the reading below.
eq_slope <- vapply(eq, function(s) {
  d <- pairs_of(s); ok <- !is.na(d$term)
  unname(stats::coef(stats::lm(d$y[ok] ~ d$term[ok]))[2])
}, numeric(1))
stopifnot(sum(eq_slope < 0) > length(eq) / 2)
ex2 |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(r2os, r2os_ct), ~ sprintf("%+.2f%%", 100 * .x)),
                     dplyr::across(c(cw, cw_ct), ~ sprintf("%.2f", .x)),
                     share_truncated = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * share_truncated))
```

The restriction helps on `r sum(ex2$r2os_ct > ex2$r2os)` of the five equity
series and binds on between
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * min(ex2$share_truncated))` and
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * max(ex2$share_truncated))` of the forecast months.
Where it helps, the unrestricted regression was producing negative forecasts
in months when the realized premium was positive, which happens when the
estimated slope has the wrong sign: @tbl-16-insample shows the term spread's
slope on `r sum(eq_slope < 0)` of the five equity series to be negative, so a steep curve pushed the
forecast below zero exactly when @fama1989 would expect the premium to be
high. Truncation cannot repair a wrong slope, but it stops the forecast from
acting on it, which is why @campbell2008 found it to be the difference between
a negative and a positive $R^2_{\text{OS}}$.

#### Exercise 3

Doubling $\kappa$ doubles every tilt until the band binds; halving it halves
them. The certainty-equivalent gain is not linear in $\kappa$, because the
variance term of @eq-16-cer is quadratic in the position.

```{r}
#| label: sol-16-ex3
ex3 <- tidyr::expand_grid(model = c("term", "mom"), mult = c(0.5, 1, 2)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(res = purrr::map2(model, mult, function(k, mlt) {
    p <- run_path(tilt_weights(fc, k, kappa = mlt * kappa0))
    tibble::tibble(turnover = 12 * mean(p$turnover), ce_gain = ce_of(p$net - rf[oos]) - ce_policy)
  })) |>
  tidyr::unnest(res)
ex3 |> dplyr::mutate(turnover = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * turnover),
                     ce_gain = sprintf("%+.0f bp", 1e4 * ce_gain))
```

```{r}
#| label: sol-16-ex3-facts
#| include: false
g3 <- function(k, mlt) ex3$ce_gain[ex3$model == k & ex3$mult == mlt]
stopifnot(all(ex3$ce_gain[ex3$model == "term"] > 0),          # gains at every scale
          all(ex3$ce_gain[ex3$model == "mom"] < 0),            # loses at every scale
          g3("term", 1) > g3("term", 0.5),                     # the term gain rises to the chapter's scale
          abs(g3("term", 2) - g3("term", 1)) < 1e-4,           # and moves by less than a basis point beyond it
          g3("mom", 1) < g3("mom", 0.5), g3("mom", 2) < g3("mom", 1),
          g3("mom", 1) - g3("mom", 2) < g3("mom", 0.5) - g3("mom", 1))   # the momentum loss grows more slowly
```

For the term spread the gain goes from
`r sprintf("%+.0f", 1e4 * g3("term", 0.5))` basis points at half the scale to
`r sprintf("%+.0f", 1e4 * g3("term", 1))` at the chapter's and
`r sprintf("%+.0f", 1e4 * g3("term", 2))` at double; for momentum from
`r sprintf("%+.0f", 1e4 * g3("mom", 0.5))` to `r sprintf("%+.0f", 1e4 * g3("mom", 1))`
to `r sprintf("%+.0f", 1e4 * g3("mom", 2))`. Neither is linear in $\kappa$.
The term-spread gain rises from half scale to the chapter's scale and then
stops, moving by less than a basis point to double, because the extra variance
and turnover absorb the extra return; the momentum loss grows from half to
full scale and again to double, but more slowly, because at double scale the
band clips more of the tilts and a clipped tilt no longer grows with $\kappa$.
The sign is first order and the size is second order: a signal with evidence
gains at every scale tried, one without loses at every scale, and the scale
should be set by the evidence rather than by the appetite.

#### Exercise 4

The timing rule holds $\hat{r}^e_{t+1}/(\gamma\hat{\sigma}^2_t)$ in
`US_equity` and the balance in the bill, with the weight confined to
$[0, 1.5]$; the comparison is a constant weight of one.

```{r}
#| label: sol-16-ex4
us <- fc[fc$series == "US_equity", ]
s2 <- as.numeric(vol60[oos - 1L, "US_equity"])^2
w  <- pmin(pmax(us$term / (gamma * s2), 0), 1.5)
r2_us <- r2_os(us$y, us$term, us$mean)
gain4 <- ce_of(w * us$y) - ce_of(us$y)
stopifnot(sign(gain4) == sign(r2_us), abs(gain4) > abs(12 * r2_us / gamma))   # same sign, realized larger
c(ce_timing = ce_of(w * us$y), ce_hold = ce_of(us$y),
  gain = ce_of(w * us$y) - ce_of(us$y),
  predicted_by_eq_ct = 12 * r2_us / gamma,
  r2os = r2_us, mean_weight = mean(w), share_at_zero = mean(w == 0))
```

The term-spread forecast of `US_equity` has an $R^2_{\text{OS}}$ of
`r sprintf("%+.2f%%", 100 * r2_us)`, so @eq-16-ct predicts a change in
expected excess return of
`r sprintf("%+.0f", 1e4 * 12 * r2_us / gamma)` basis points a year, and the
realized certainty-equivalent gain is
`r sprintf("%+.0f", 1e4 * (ce_of(w * us$y) - ce_of(us$y)))` basis points. The
two agree in sign and the realized figure is the larger in magnitude, because
@eq-16-ct is a first-order approximation for an unconstrained position while
this rule is clipped at zero and at one and a half, spends
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(w == 0))` of its months in the bill, and holds
an average weight of `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(w))` rather than one. An absolute
view on a series whose forecast loses to its own mean is a bet against the
mean, and it costs what @eq-16-ct says it should.
